title: Error correction and quantum information spreading on sparse random graphs
authors: Giovanni Cemin, Marin Bukov, Andrea Solfanelli
abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes on graph geometries beyond regular euclidean lattices have emerged as a promising route toward robust quantum information processing. A major challenge in quantum error correction is the trade-off between favorable properties of codes constructed in high dimensionality and the need for locality in practical implementations on near-term hardware. Sparse intermediate geometries may combine the advantages of both, but how their structure governs quantum information dynamics and code performance remains unclear. Here we show that the spectral dimension $d_s$, defined from the low-energy spectrum of the graph Laplacian, is the universal parameter connecting these properties. Using Floquet random Clifford circuits on two distinct sparse graph architectures with tunable spectral dimension, we find that $d_s$ governs both quantum information spreading and the scaling of the resulting quantum error-correcting code distance. We identify a geometry-induced entanglement phase transition from localized area-law to ergodic volume-law, whose universality is determined by $d_s$ and exhibits long-range percolation criticality. In the ergodic phase, the circuit acts as a CSS code encoder whose code distance is set by the competition between two logical sectors --- the cost of severing the graph and the length of its shortest winding cycle --- which connectivity pushes in opposite directions. The spectral dimension organizes this trade-off, highlighting a maximum at intermediate $d_s$ retaining sparse connectivity and physical realizability.
summary: This work establishes the spectral dimension ($d_s$) as the universal metric controlling quantum information dynamics on sparse random graphs. It shows that $d_s$ governs the transition between localized and ergodic entanglement regimes and optimizes the trade-off in quantum error-correcting code distance. This provides a crucial theoretical tool for designing robust quantum hardware based on engineered connectivity.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the underlying structure of an interaction graph dictates the dynamics of quantum information and the performance limits of quantum error-correcting codes (QEC) on non-Euclidean geometries.
main_result: The spectral dimension ($d_s$) of the graph is identified as the universal parameter governing both quantum information spreading (area-law vs. volume-law entanglement) and the scaling of the QEC code distance.
method: The analysis uses Floquet random Clifford circuits on sparse random graphs, relating spectral properties (via the graph Laplacian) to entanglement measures and code distance scaling.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum many-body systems whose interactions are defined by a sparse random graph. Dynamics are simulated using Floquet random Clifford circuits containing both blocking and non-blocking gates.
key_observables: Spectral dimension ($d_s$), entanglement entropy scaling (area-law vs. volume-law), and the achievable code distance.
important_parameters: The spectral dimension ($d_s$), which is determined by the graph's connectivity structure and the balance between competing error channels (graph cuts vs. winding cycles).
main_assumptions: The framework extends concepts from classical complex networks to non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, assuming implementability on platforms like neutral atoms.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the Floquet random circuit on the LR and PWR2 graphs. Other figures relate to the cutting probability $P_{cut}(i)$ and the spectral gap scaling.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting the limitations of Euclidean lattices, introduces $d_s$ as the key parameter, and then analyzes how $d_s$ controls the entanglement transition (percolation) and optimizes the trade-off in QEC code distance scaling.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, universal geometric diagnostic ($d_s$) to predict fundamental quantum properties (like error resilience) in complex, engineered quantum hardware architectures.
